Subjection
sub-JEK-shun
n.
From Latin subjectio, a placing under, from sub plus jacere, to throw. Webster 1828: the act of subduing; the state of being under the power or authority of another. In the New Testament the Greek is a military word for ranking under, and it governs Christ’s dominion, the church’s order, and a man’s rule over his own body.

Biblical Definition

The New Testament uses subjection for an ordered placing under, and its widest use is christological. Hebrews quotes the eighth psalm: Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him (Hebrews 2:8) — the dominion is granted, the visible fulfilment is not yet complete, and the writer resolves the tension by pointing to Jesus crowned with glory. The same chapter notes that unto the angels hath he not put in subjection the world to come (Hebrews 2:5). Then the ordered applications. Paul disciplines himself: I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway (1 Corinthians 9:27). An overseer must be one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity (1 Timothy 3:4). Women are to learn in silence with all subjection in the assembly (1 Timothy 2:11), and wives are to be in subjection to your own husbands (1 Peter 3:1). And Paul refuses it where the gospel is at stake: To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you (Galatians 2:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SUBJECTION as the act of subduing; the act of bringing under the dominion of another; and the state of being under the power, control, and government of another. The Greek adds the idea of ordered rank rather than crushed resistance.

expand to see more

SUBJECTION, n. — The act of subduing; the act of vanquishing and bringing under the dominion of another.

The state of being under the power, control and government of another; as, the safety of life, liberty and property consists in our subjection to the laws.

Webster’s second illustration is the biblical instinct. Subjection is not the opposite of freedom; a lawless society is not free. The New Testament word is drawn from military ranking — a soldier placed in his order — which is why it can be used of the Son to the Father without any thought of inferiority of being.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 9:27 — "But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway."

Galatians 2:5 — "To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you."

1 Timothy 3:4 — "One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;"

Hebrews 2:8 — "Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet. For in that he put all in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him. But now we see not yet all things put under him."

1 Peter 3:1 — "Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;"

Modern Corruption

Subjection is corrupted by egalitarian readings that treat every ordered relation as oppression, and equally by abusers who quote 1 Peter 3:1 while ignoring the verses that bind the husband — the first denies the order, the second denies its terms.

expand to see more

The creational order of headship and submission between husband and wife is taught in Genesis 2, argued from creation in 1 Corinthians 11:3-9, applied in Ephesians 5:22-33, and repeated by Peter in 1 Peter 3:1-7. The egalitarian reading treats these as culturally bound accommodations that the gospel itself overturns, usually appealing to Galatians 3:28. But Galatians 3:28 concerns standing before God in justification, not the abolition of created office, and Paul who wrote it also wrote 1 Timothy 2:11-15 and grounded it in the order of creation rather than in Ephesian custom. The dictionary’s reference standard on this is the biblical-order entry, and the treatment of egalitarianism as a corruption of the creational pattern is stated there.

The second corruption is more wicked and more common in practice. 1 Peter 3:1 is quoted at wives by men who never read to verse 7, where the husband is commanded to dwell with his wife according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, on pain of having his prayers hindered — nor to Ephesians 5:25, where he is told to love her as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it. Headship in Scripture is defined by a Husband who died. A man who uses these texts to demand and not to spend himself has inverted them, and the elders of a church are bound to say so. The same chapter that requires an overseer to have his children in subjection with all gravity (1 Timothy 3:4) disqualifies the striker and the brawler two verses earlier.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Greek hupotasso is a military term meaning to arrange under, to rank beneath; its noun hupotage is the New Testament’s subjection. It denotes ordered place, not enforced defeat, except where the context is conquest.

expand to see more

Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to arrange under, to subordinate, to place in rank beneath; used of Christ’s dominion, of wives, of citizens, and of the Son to the Father in 1 Corinthians 15:28.

Greek hupotage (G5292) — subjection, subordination; learn in silence with all subjection (1 Timothy 2:11), subjection unto the gospel of Christ (2 Corinthians 9:13).

Greek doulagogeo (G1396) — to lead as a slave, to bring under control; bring it into subjection of Paul’s own body (1 Corinthians 9:27).

Hebrews 2:8 quotes Psalm 8:6 in the Septuagint, where hupotasso renders the Hebrew for putting under the feet.

The middle voice of hupotasso is used of the wife in 1 Peter 3:1 — a voluntary ranking of oneself, not a subjugation imposed.

Usage

"Thou hast put all things in subjection under his feet… But now we see not yet all things put under him (Hebrews 2:8) — the dominion granted and not yet visibly complete."

"I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27) — the apostle’s own discipline, lest he be a castaway."

"We gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour (Galatians 2:5) — where the gospel is at stake, subjection is refused outright."
